comments.author: @Talisk3r
comments.text:
So your calculation is that, if you have enough money, you can simply buy your way out of trouble, even as the scale and pace of environmental problems keep increasing?

We never really establish the actual cost of fixing these problems. Those costs are either externalized by accountants or estimated by environmental consultants. And since solutions are rarely implemented, the real costs remain theoretical and easy to ignore.

I genuinely appreciate your work, but I think this reliance on the optionality that wealth provides, rather than tackling the underlying problems (environmental degradation, class conflict), is precisely what has brought us here.

Environmental crises don't respect national borders. Entire regions can be affected, and neighbouring countries may exploit the situation rather than offer assistance. You need to consider regional interdependence, political relationships and competing interests, not just individual countries.

When assessing environmental risks, I'd put less weight on national debt and currency strength, and more on a country's resources, institutions, climatic region, neighbours and actual sovereignty. Countries are interconnected, but some are far more dependent on their neighbours and trading partners than others.

I also think you're assuming that a crisis will hurt one country while leaving others relatively unscathed, allowing them to benefit from their financial position. But what happens when the crisis is regional or global? Wealth and currency strength can't necessarily buy resources, functioning infrastructure, political stability or cooperation when everyone is competing for the same things.

If your main concern is an economic downturn, you're right on the money ;-). But even your "green" countries will likely experience stagflation.
